title: The sages' own prayers (Berakhot 16b–17a)
hookLine: a page of personal prayers; one became the Amidah's closing prayer
tomorrow: how can a grown man say he's 'as if unformed'?

cards: The notes app on a phone is full of things nobody else will read. Half a poem. A text that never got sent.
A sentence written at one in the morning. One page of the Talmud reads like that. The tractate has been talking about the Amidah, the standing prayer, the words everyone shares.
Then, without warning, it opens the sages' versions folder: what each of them said after the shared words were done.

teach.b: Here's the page, in plain words. Rabbi Elazar, finishing his prayer, asked that love and brotherhood, peace and friendship would live among his people.
Rabbi Yochanan asked God to look at their shame and see their trouble. Rabbi Alexandri was blunt.

Our will is to do Your will, he said, so what stops us? The yeast in the dough, and the rule of foreign kingdoms. Each prayer sounds like the person who said it, pressed out of whatever was weighing on him that day.
Then comes Mar, son of Ravina.
My God, he said, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit. To those who curse me, let my soul be silent. Open my heart to Your Torah.
He's leaning on a psalm: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." And here's the part to tell a friend tonight. Mar's private words didn't stay private.

teach.h: NOW IN THE SIDDUR: ELOHAI NETZOR.
teach.b: They now sit in the siddur, the prayer book, at the very end of the Amidah, beginning Elohai netzor: my God, guard. One man's own line, said after the shared words, became shared words.
So on this page, the fixed prayer and your own prayer aren't rivals. The sages said the prayer everyone says, then kept going in their own voice.

how: In the siddur, Elohai netzor follows the Amidah, and the end of the Amidah is a place where a person may add a private request in their own words before stepping back.

games.q: what does “the sages' own prayers” mean?
o: the rules the sages set for who may lead a prayer
personal prayers the sages added after the fixed one
prayers the sages' students wrote down in their name

s: Jewish prayer is only fixed words; there's no room for your own
on this page the sages say the shared prayer, then add their own.
a private prayer of Mar son of Ravina now closes the Amidah
it begins Elohai netzor, my God, guard my tongue.
every sage on the page asks for the same thing
love and peace, shame seen, the yeast in the dough: each sounds like its sage.

games.q: your teammate keeps meaning to call his dad and never does. if he prayed the way Rabbi Alexandri did, what would he say?
o: here's what i want to do, and here's what keeps stopping me.
only the fixed words, and nothing about the call at all.
a promise that he'll never let it slip again, starting now.
games.why: Alexandri: our will is to do Your will, so what stops us? the yeast in the dough. his prayer names the obstacle honestly.

practice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write one sentence of your own, the way the sages did once the shared words were done: to God if you pray, or as a plain hope if you don't. Keep it short enough to fold into a pocket.

wordCard.voice: The sages' own prayers. A page of Berakhot where each sage adds his own words, and one of them, Elohai netzor, ends up in the siddur.

orig.note: Hebrew: my God, guard. the opening of Mar son of Ravina's prayer, now at the end of the Amidah.

carryVoice: Your line: your own prayer. Mar's private sentence now closes the Amidah. Twelve of fifty in Berakhot.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 16b–17a (prayers the sages said after their Amidah: Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Alexandri, Mar son of Ravina)

sources.q: Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.
